Each FOL statement seems to correctly correspond to its natural language counterpart, assuming standard interpretations of the predicates and logical connectives. For example, negations match 'not', implications match 'if...then', disjunctions match 'or', and exclusive or (⊕') matches 'either...or but not both', which is acceptable under a charitable reading. The universal quantifier is also correctly interpreted. The last statement 'If Asaiah displays bravery, then he will save lives.' maps to p_5 → p_6, which is consistent given p_5 is 'displays bravery', and p_6 plausibly means 'will save lives'. google/gemini-2.5-flash.mistake: The mistake is in statements 7 and 12. In both cases, the natural language phrase 'either...or..., but not necessarily both' implies an inclusive OR (∨), meaning at least one of the conditions is true. However, the FOL statement uses the exclusive OR (⊕), which means exactly one of the conditions is true (one or the other, but not both). The 'not necessarily both' in the NL directly contradicts the 'not both' part of the exclusive OR. If the NL had simply said 'either...or..., but not both' then ⊕ would be correct. If the NL meant to convey inclusive OR, using ⊕ was an error. Given the phrase 'not necessarily both', inclusive OR (∨) would be the correct logical operator.
